parts.title: Reporting a lost bag
parts.context: A woman phones a railway station's lost property office to report a lost rucksack.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a railway station to report a lost bag. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Kingsmead Central Station, lost property office. Martin speaking.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Oh, hello. Um, I'm hoping you can help me. I think I left my rucksack on a train yesterday, and I wondered if anyone had handed it in.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Don't worry, we get a lot of bags handed in. I'll just start filling in a report form.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman has lost a rucksack, so 'rucksack' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Right. Can I take your name, please?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Yes. It's Hannah Lindqvist.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Of course. It's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T. It's a Swedish name, so people always get it wrong.
script.tts: Of course. It's L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T. It's a Swedish name, so people always get it wrong.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Thank you. And what's the best number to reach you on?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: My mobile is 07700 900 316. Oh, sorry, I've swapped the last two digits. It's 361.
script.tts: My mobile is oh seven seven double oh, nine double oh, three one six. Oh, sorry, I've swapped the last two digits. It's three six one.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: So that's 07700 900 361. Is that right?
script.tts: So that's oh seven seven double oh, nine double oh, three six one. Is that right?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Yes, that's it.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Lovely. And what date did you travel on?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Yesterday. That was the fourteenth. No, hang on, today's the sixteenth, isn't it? So it was the fifteenth. Sorry, I've lost track of the days this week.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: No problem. And which train were you on?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Well, I started out at Westerby, but I had to change at Dunmore, and I left the rucksack on the second train, the one from Dunmore to here.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: I see. And what time did that train leave Dunmore?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: I usually catch the quarter to nine, but I missed it this time, so I took the next one, at nine twenty.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Right, thanks. And do you remember where you put the bag?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Um, up on the rack above my seat, I think. I got off in a hurry, because my meeting started in half an hour.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: That's the most likely place, yes. OK, I think that's everything for the journey. Now I just need a description of the bag.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: So, what does the rucksack look like?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: It's a medium-sized one, dark green, with a grey stripe down the front. Oh, no, sorry, that's my brother's. Mine is dark blue. The stripe's grey on both, though.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: OK. And is there anything on it that would help us recognise it? A name label, for instance?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: I took the label off ages ago. But there's a little metal keyring clipped to the zip, and it's a tiny lighthouse. I bought it on holiday years ago.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Lovely. And what was inside? Anything valuable?

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Mostly clothes, and a couple of textbooks. My laptop's at home, thank goodness. But there's a camera in a padded case, and that's what worries me most. It belongs to my university department.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: I'll put all that on the report. Now, if it has been handed in, it'll be brought down to us. The station's a big place, so let me explain. The main entrance is next to platform one, but we're at the far end of the concourse, beside platform six, just past the ticket machines.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Right. And is there a charge for collecting it?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Yes, there's a handling charge. We keep everything here for ten days, and after that it's sent to the central depot, where the charge is higher. If you collect it from us, it's five pounds, and you can only pay by card, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: That's fine. Thank you very much for your help.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: You're welcome. We'll text you as soon as it turns up. Goodbye.

script.speaker: hannah
script.text: Goodbye.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Welcome to a new sports centre
parts.context: The manager of a new community sports centre welcomes local people on its open day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a new community sports centre welcoming local people on its open day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Harbourside Community Sports Centre. I'm Nina Brennan, the manager. It's lovely to see so many of you at our first open day. Before I show you round, a few words about how the centre came about.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Some of you may have read that it grew out of a council survey. Well, that isn't quite right. It began with a group of local parents, who were tired of driving their children to another town just to find a swimming pool. They started a petition, and only when they'd collected five thousand signatures did the council agree to pay. The athletics club backed the campaign too, but it was the parents who got it started.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Now, the building itself. We tried to make it as green as possible. There are solar panels on the roof, but they only power the lighting. The pool is a different story. Next door is a commercial laundry, which gives off huge amounts of hot air every day, and until now that heat was simply wasted. We've fitted pipes to capture it, and it now keeps the whole pool warm. We did consider a heat pump, but that would have cost twice as much.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Now, membership. Everybody who joins gets a fitness assessment, so that's not a special offer. Last month we were also waiving the joining fee, but I'm afraid that has ended. What we're offering this month is different: if you sign up before the end of June, you can bring a friend free of charge for your first four weeks.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: A word about classes. You can book up to a week ahead. I know many of you will want to ring us, but we've stopped taking phone bookings, because the line was always busy. You can book at the front desk, but there's often a queue, so I'd strongly recommend downloading our app.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: And finally, can teenagers use the gym? Yes, from the age of fourteen. A parent doesn't need to stay with them, and they don't need a letter from school. What they do need is to attend an induction session with one of our instructors before their first visit. After that, they're free to use it on their own.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Now let me tell you where everything is. Please look at the plan of the ground floor. You're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan. Reception is straight away on your left, where you'll collect your membership cards.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Opposite reception, on the right, is our café, which opens at seven every morning. Next to the café, on its far side, is the physiotherapy room, but that won't open until the autumn.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Now walk straight ahead along the main corridor until you reach a junction. The swimming pool is straight in front of you. Turn left, and the first room on your left is the fitness gym. Directly opposite the gym, across the main corridor, are the squash courts, but they're not ready yet.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Carry on to the end of the corridor. The last room on the left is the dance studio, with mirrors on three walls. The big room on the right is the sports hall.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Back at the junction, if you turn right instead, you'll pass the swimming pool on your left. At the far end, the large room on your left is the climbing wall. And directly opposite it, on the right, you'll find the crèche, where children from six months old are looked after while you exercise.

script.speaker: nina
script.text: Right, that's all from me. Tours leave from reception every quarter of an hour, so do have a look around.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A field-trip report on rock pools
parts.context: Two marine biology students discuss a field-trip report with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two marine biology students, Tessa and Callum, talking to their tutor, Dr Hughes, about a report on a field trip to a rocky shore. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Come in, both of you. I've read your draft report, and on the whole it's very good. Let's start with the site. Why Kelby Point? I'd have thought Seaton would have been easier, with the bus stopping right outside.

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: It would have been easier to get to, yes. But Seaton is mostly sand, with just a few small pools. At Kelby the rocks run from the top of the shore right down to the low-tide line, so there are pools at several different heights.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: And that mattered, because the whole point was to compare them. Dr Cooper did mention Kelby to us, but that wasn't why we picked it.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Fine. Now, did everything go to plan on the day?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Well, um, not quite. The weather was lovely, and the equipment all worked. But we'd got the tide table wrong by about an hour, so the water came back faster than we expected, and we only half finished the two lowest pools.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: I see. And what did you make of the results overall?

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: Well, we expected the number of species to go up steadily as you go down the shore, because the lower pools are covered by the sea for longer. And the upper pools did have the fewest, mostly just a few periwinkles and some seaweed.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: But what surprised us was the middle shore. We thought it would be somewhere between the other two, but it had almost as many species as the lowest pools. Eleven, compared with twelve.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: That's worth highlighting. Now, presentation. You've put all your raw counts in the main text, sixty-odd lines of numbers. Was that deliberate?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: That was my idea, actually. I thought readers would want to check every figure.

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: But it makes the results section really long, and the graphs get lost.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Tessa's right. Readers want to see the pattern first, so I'd move the raw data to an appendix and keep a short summary table in the main text.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: OK, that makes sense. I'll do that.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: And what about those two pools you only half surveyed? What did you do with those figures?

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: We left them out of the analysis, but we didn't say so anywhere in the report. Should we go back and finish them?

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: There isn't time before the deadline, and you don't need to. But don't hide it. Say what happened, and put it in your limitations section. Markers respect honesty far more than a tidy-looking result.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Right. Now let's go through the species section. Limpets first.

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: They were the easiest to survey, because each limpet stays on its own patch of rock. We found them in every single pool, from the top of the shore to the bottom.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Good. And the starfish?

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Those were only found in the lowest pools. We didn't see a single one higher up, which makes sense, because they can't cope with being out of the water for long.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: What about the shore crabs?

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: They were the hardest to count, because they hide under rocks and in the seaweed. So our figures are probably an underestimate.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: And periwinkles? I thought you said there was something odd there.

script.speaker: callum
script.text: Yes. There were far fewer than in the last survey of Kelby Point, ten years ago. We wondered if the warm weather had affected them, but the temperatures were normal for the time of year. So we think people may be collecting them to eat. We can't prove it, though.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: Interesting. And the prawns?

script.speaker: tessa
script.text: We saw lots of them, but they move about so fast that we kept losing count. In the end we just recorded them as present or absent.

script.speaker: hughes
script.text: That's fine. Right, send me the revised version by Friday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: urban beekeeping and pollination
parts.context: A lecture about keeping bees in cities and what it means for pollination.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about keeping bees in cities and why it matters for pollination. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. In today's session on urban ecology, I want to look at something that has become a surprisingly common sight in our cities: the beehive. Look down from almost any tall building and you'll spot them, up on the rooftops of offices, hotels and even theatres. Beekeeping in cities has boomed over the last ten years, and I want to ask two questions. Is it good for the bees? And is it good for the plants that depend on them?

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Let's start with the bees themselves. A honeybee colony can contain fifty thousand workers in midsummer. They fly out to collect nectar, which they turn into honey, and pollen, which feeds the young. A worker will usually forage within about two kilometres of the hive. Sorry, nearer three, actually. In a city, that means thousands of gardens, parks and balconies within reach.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why might a city suit bees better than the countryside? There are three main reasons. First, variety. A large arable farm may grow only one crop, say sunflowers, which flower for a few weeks and then leave the bees with nothing. A city has gardens, street trees and parks, so something is in flower almost all year round, from snowdrops in February to ivy in October. Second, temperature. Buildings and roads hold heat, so a city can be a couple of degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. Plants flower earlier and carry on later, so the season is considerably longer. And third, chemicals. Farmers have to protect huge areas of crops, and they use a lot of pesticides. Most gardeners use far less, and some city councils have banned them from public parks altogether.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now, what does this have to do with pollination? When a bee lands on a flower, tiny grains of pollen stick to the branched hairs covering its body. When it flies to the next flower, some of those grains rub off, and the flower can be fertilised and produce seeds or fruit. Many of the foods we eat depend on this, including apples, strawberries and beans. And bees have a remarkable way of sharing information. When a worker finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs what we call a waggle dance. The angle of the dance tells the others which direction to fly in, and its length tells them how far to go.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: However, urban beekeeping isn't without problems. The first is competition. Honeybees are very efficient foragers, and in a city with too many hives there may not be enough flowers to go round. A three-year study in the northern city of Ashgrove compared districts with many hives and districts with few. In the crowded districts, researchers counted noticeably fewer wild bumblebees, which suggests that the honeybees were taking their food. The second problem is disease. A tiny parasite called the varroa mite feeds on honeybees and spreads viruses between colonies, and those viruses can then pass to wild bees visiting the same flowers. The third problem worries neighbours rather than bees. In early summer, when a colony outgrows its hive, the old queen leaves with about half the workers to find a new home. This is called swarming. A swarm looks frightening, but the bees are actually very gentle at that stage, because they have no honey or young to defend.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So what can be done? Beekeepers can help by not keeping too many hives in one area, and by checking their colonies regularly for disease. Hives on roofs also need a source of water close by. Bees use it to cool the hive in hot weather, and a roof has no ponds or puddles, so a shallow dish with pebbles in it is essential. Shade is useful too, but water is the thing they can't manage without. And cities themselves can help. Councils could plant more lime trees along streets. Their flowers are rich in nectar, and they bloom in July, just when many other plants have finished. Oak and cherry trees are attractive, but oak gives almost no nectar and cherry blossom comes much earlier in the spring.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: To sum up, used carefully, urban beekeeping can benefit both bees and plants. Next week, we'll look at the honey itself, and why city honey can taste so different from one neighbourhood to the next.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
